# The Fence

Emma had always prided herself on her athletic ability. At thirteen, she could outrun most kids in her grade, and jumping fences was practically her signature move. So when her best friend Maya dared her to take the shortcut through Miller's property instead of walking around it, Emma didn't hesitate.

The white picket fence was nothing—probably only five feet high. She'd cleared taller obstacles during gym class.

She backed up a few steps to get her running start, her sundress swishing around her legs. The yellow fabric was her favorite, light and perfect for the warm spring afternoon. She sprinted forward, planted her hand on the top rail, and pushed off.

For a perfect moment, she was airborne, free.

Then she felt it—a terrible *catch* and *tear*.

Her dress had snagged on one of the fence's decorative post toppers, the kind with a pointed finial. As her body weight pulled downward, the fabric caught and ripped viciously. Emma landed hard on the other side, breathless, and immediately looked back.

Her dress was gone.

Not entirely—it dangled from the fence, a pathetic yellow flag of her humiliation. What remained were the straps, still attached to her shoulders, barely covering anything. She looked down at herself in absolute horror.

She was wearing her plain white underwear and her training bra. Nothing else.

For a second, Emma stood frozen, her mind unable to fully process what had happened. Heat flooded her face so intensely she thought she might be sick.

*No, no, no, no, no.*

She crossed her arms over her chest and looked frantically around. The yard was empty, but she was completely exposed to the street on the other side of the fence, and to any window in the neighboring houses.

Tears pricked her eyes. How was she going to get home? She lived six blocks away. Even if she ran, people would see her. The neighborhood park was nearby—families went there on Saturday afternoons.

Her breathing started to get shallow. This was actually happening. This was the worst thing that had ever happened.

She heard the squeak of a gate opening from the house behind her.

Emma's head snapped around. An older man—maybe her grandfather's age—stepped into the yard, carrying a watering can. He had gray hair and kind-looking blue eyes, and he was looking directly at her.

Emma felt her face go completely white. She dropped her arms to her sides in panic, then immediately crossed them again, her mortification reaching new heights. She was sure she resembled a tomato at this point—her whole body felt like it was on fire.

The man's expression shifted from confusion to understanding in about two seconds. His eyes darted to the torn dress hanging on the fence, then back to her face. To his credit, his expression became very carefully neutral. He didn't smile or make any gesture that might have seemed mocking.

"Well," he said calmly, as if finding a panicked girl in his yard in her underwear was a normal Saturday occurrence, "I think we should fix this situation."

He turned and walked back into his house through the sliding glass door without another word.

Emma wanted to disappear entirely. She wanted to dissolve into the ground like morning dew. He'd *seen* her. A complete stranger had seen her like this. She wanted to run, but run where? She was trapped.

The man reappeared after what felt like an eternity but was probably only thirty seconds. He held out a navy blue windbreaker jacket—the kind older people wore to golf outings.

"It's clean," he said gently, still maintaining that careful neutrality. "I just wore it last week."

Emma's eyes stung with grateful tears. She wanted to die of embarrassment, but she also wanted this kind man to know she wasn't a complete idiot. She uncrossed her arms and took the jacket with trembling hands.

"Thank you," she whispered, immediately putting it on. It hung to her mid-thigh, large enough to cover everything. She'd never been more grateful for anything in her life.

"What's your name?" the man asked.

"Emma."

"I'm Mr. Patterson. This is my house." He gestured to the fence. "That's quite a snag. Was it the finial?"

Emma nodded miserably, still not quite able to make eye contact. "I was taking a shortcut."

"Well," Mr. Patterson said, "I'd come help you retrieve your dress, but I suspect you'd prefer privacy. There's a gate around the side of the fence—it opens to the street. You can go around and collect it from the front side. I'll go inside."

He turned to head back in, then paused. "And Emma? Don't be too hard on yourself. Everyone has an embarrassing moment. Most people are too wrapped up in their own worries to judge you as harshly as you're judging yourself."

He went inside, sliding the door closed behind him.

Emma stood there in his oversized jacket, in her yard, while the afternoon sun shone down on her. The embarrassment still burned hot in her cheeks, but something else was there too—gratitude, and a strange kind of relief.

She walked to the gate and retrieved her dress, carefully folding it despite the giant tear down the side. She'd have to explain this to her mother somehow. That would be its own kind of embarrassing.

But as she walked home in Mr. Patterson's jacket, she realized the awful, burning shame was already beginning to fade. The moment had been horrible and ridiculous, yes. But Mr. Patterson was right about one thing: he'd handled it with such kindness that she'd actually have to work hard to relive the embarrassment tomorrow.

She'd return his jacket carefully cleaned. She might even tell him he was right.
